sections.overview: Elephas maximus is Asia’s largest living land mammal. Smaller than African elephants, it survives in scattered populations. Its grasping trunk and massive body support foraging across varied landscapes.
sections.identification: Adults have grey skin, sometimes pink on the ears, forehead or trunk; young are hairier and reddish. They have smaller, rounder ears than African elephants and one finger-like trunk tip. Only some males grow prominent tusks; many lack them, while females and some males have short tushes. Tusk frequency varies among populations. Adult Asian elephants typically stand 1.8–3.8 m at the shoulder and weigh about 2,750–5,420 kg; males are usually larger than females. The cited institutional account does not give a body-width measurement.
sections.habitat: It survives in fragmented parts of South and Southeast Asia, including India, Sri Lanka, Sumatra and Borneo. Habitats include evergreen and deciduous forests, thorn scrub, grasslands and modified landscapes. It forages in forest clearings and moves widely for food and water.
sections.diet: This herbivore eats grasses, leaves, roots, vines, shoots, twigs, bark and fruit. Its diet shifts with habitat and season; studies in southern India found more browse in the dry season. It feeds for much of the day because digestion extracts only part of food energy.
sections.behavior: Related females and young form matrilineal communities; groups may split and reunite while foraging. Young males leave their natal group; adults are often solitary or associate with males. Elephants communicate through scent, touch and low-frequency calls, and explore objects with the trunk.
sections.reproduction: Females usually have their first calf in their teens. Gestation lasts about 21.5–22 months; births are usually single, though twins occur. Calves stand and nurse soon after birth, then eat vegetation at about six months. Several years separate births, depending on environmental conditions.
sections.ecology: Elephants disperse seeds far from parent plants. In a Kerala evergreen forest, a study found viable seeds of 27 woody species in dung; ingested seeds germinated sooner than controls. This shows seed dispersal at that site, without implying identical effects across the species’ range.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment published in 2020 classified the species as Endangered, based on a 2019 assessment. It inferred a decline of at least 50% over three generations, linked to habitat loss and degradation. Fragmentation blocks movement routes and brings elephants near farms and settlements. These data belong to that dated global assessment.
